role: kabir - Red Team (defensive OWASP security audit), RC 115f698
summary: Defensive audit of RC 115f698 (clean checkout at C:/Users/Sage world/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/rc-115f698). The codebase has clearly been through several hardening rounds: JWT HS256 with fail-closed secret validation, refresh rotation, HttpOnly SameSite refresh cookie, explicit CORS allow-list, CSP, constant-time HMAC on every webhook, server-derived escrow/top-up amounts, SSRF guard with DNS pinning, magic-byte upload sniffing plus ClamAV in prod, parameterised queries throughout, and scoped workspace lookups on every id-taking endpoint I sampled. Still NOT go-live clean. Two P0s: (1) live-format credentials are committed in tracked example files: an Anthropic key and a Sarvam key in influora-ai/env.example, Cloudflare R2 access-key/secret and MSG91 keys in influora-api/env.example, all present in git history across 3-5 commits (values not printed). (2) The /internal/** service-mesh gate (InternalServiceTokenFilter) matches the RAW request URI, so a percent-encoded path such as /api/v1/%69nternal/meera/turns/release skips the service-token and HMAC checks while Spring MVC still routes it to MeeraInternalController. I reproduced this with the exact spring-web 6.1.14 and spring-security-web 6.3.4 jars the RC uses: StrictHttpFirewall ALLOWS it, the filter does not run, and MVC routes it to the controller. A logged-in brand therefore needs only its own access JWT plus the on-behalf token the browser already receives, and can refund every Meera turn credit (free AI usage on the platform's bill) or write forged assistant messages. P1s: any brand member, VIEWER included, can approve a deliverable, and approval releases escrow money even though the explicit release endpoint requires OWNER/ADMIN. An admin access token can silently replace an already-enabled MFA secret (persistent takeover, or lockout of the real admin). Admin login has no IP rate limit. On the deploy/utho topology (nginx -> Caddy -> Tomcat RemoteIpValve), every client IP collapses to the Docker gateway, so per-IP limits become global limits. P2s: login endpoints reveal whether an account exists and its type before checking the password; password-reset and invite tokens sit in URLs on pages that load GTM (GA4/Clarity/Meta Pixel); contract signing and webhook-secret rotation have no role checks; account deletion needs no re-authentication.

questions.question: Can a non-service caller reach /internal/meera/* without the dual service-token + HMAC credential?
questions.why_it_matters: These routes refund AI credits, persist assistant turns and run write tools (create_campaign, request_payment, confirm_launch) on behalf of a workspace.
questions.answer: Yes, via percent-encoding. InternalServiceTokenFilter.doFilterInternal (InternalServiceTokenFilter.java:82-83) runs stripContext(request.getRequestURI()).startsWith("/internal/") on the RAW URI and does no decoding. Spring MVC's PathPatternParser matches on decoded segments. MeeraInternalController has no secondary InternalPrincipal/ROLE_INTERNAL_SERVICE check, and SecurityConfig puts /internal/** under anyRequest().authenticated(), which any user JWT satisfies.
questions.evidence: Runtime probe with spring-web 6.1.14 + spring-security-web 6.3.4 + tomcat-embed-core 10.1.31, the same versions as spring-boot 3.3.5 (pom.xml:10). Result: '/api/v1/%69nternal/meera/turns/release firewall=ALLOWED internalFilterRuns=false mvcRoutesToController=true'. Control URI '/api/v1/internal/...' gives internalFilterRuns=true. No InternalServiceTokenFilter test exists in src/test or target/surefire-reports.
questions.remaining_uncertainty: Not replayed end-to-end against a booted app. Caddy/nginx might normalise %69 before proxying (Caddy passes the escaped path through by default, and nginx proxy_pass without a URI part forwards the original request line).

questions.question: Are any real credentials committed in the RC tree or in the history of tracked env/example files?
questions.why_it_matters: Anyone with repo access, or any leak of the repo, gets working third-party credentials: LLM spend, object-storage read/write of uploads including KYC documents, and transactional email/SMS.
questions.answer: Yes. influora-ai/env.example:12 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is a 108-char sk-ant-...AA value (entropy 5.49, no placeholder markers). influora-ai/env.example:19 SARVAM_API_KEY is 36 chars, high entropy. influora-api/env.example:50-51 hold R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID (32 hex) and R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY (64 hex), the exact Cloudflare R2 credential format. influora-api/env.example:67 and :71 hold MSG91_AUTH_KEY and MSG91_TOKEN_AUTH (27 alnum each). The influora-ai file carries the same values in 5 commits (b63ccf3 through 8c7b18b); influora-api/env.example has 3 commits (b63ccf3, 8c7b18b, 864971a). Values not printed.
questions.evidence: git grep for key patterns plus a python shape/entropy analysis of the RC tree and of git show <commit>:influora-ai/env.example for every commit.
questions.remaining_uncertainty: I did not test whether the keys are live, because that would call third-party APIs with them. Their shape and entropy match real keys, not placeholders.

questions.question: Does every money-moving brand action enforce the same workspace role as the explicit escrow endpoints?
questions.why_it_matters: Brand teams have VIEWER/MEMBER seats. If a low-role seat can move money, the brand has no real separation of duties.
questions.answer: No. EscrowService.release/refund (EscrowService.java:593-595, 946-948) require OWNER/ADMIN. BrandDeliverableService.approve (BrandDeliverableService.java:128-187) calls only brandContext.requireBrandWorkspace (JWT claim, no membership or role check) and then escrowService.tryReleaseOnApproval(workspaceId, milestoneId), which releases escrow to the creator. ContractService.recordSignature (ContractService.java:897-904) calls requireMember with no requireRole, while generate/amend/cancel require OWNER/ADMIN/MANAGER.
questions.evidence: Direct code read. MemberRole enum = OWNER, ADMIN, MANAGER, MEMBER, VIEWER. BrandDeliverableServiceTest/ControllerTest contain no role assertion for approve (grep for VIEWER/MemberRole found only EscrowServiceRelease* tests).
questions.remaining_uncertainty: Not runtime-reproduced. The product may intend approve to be open to all members, but then the explicit OWNER/ADMIN release gate is meaningless.

questions.question: Is admin MFA robust against a stolen admin access token?
questions.why_it_matters: Admin tokens live in localStorage (src/admin/services/admin-session.ts:107), so one XSS or a stolen token must not become a persistent takeover.
questions.answer: No. AdminAuthService.setupMfa (AdminAuthService.java:278-291) calls admin.stageMfaSecret(), which overwrites encrypted_mfa_secret (AdminUser.java:242-245) even when mfaEnabled is already true. It does not require the current TOTP code or the password. login() then verifies against the new secret (AdminAuthService.java:152). A 15-minute access token can therefore re-bind MFA to an attacker's authenticator and keep access. Calling setup alone also locks the real admin out.
questions.evidence: Direct code read; there is no guard on isMfaEnabled() in setupMfa, and no test calls setupMfa.
questions.remaining_uncertainty: The attacker still needs the admin's password to log in later. The rebind converts a short-lived token theft into a durable second factor, and immediately breaks the real admin's MFA.

questions.question: Is admin login rate-limited per IP?
questions.why_it_matters: It is the highest-value credential endpoint.
questions.answer: No. AuthRateLimitFilter.bucketFor (AuthRateLimitFilter.java:342-512) buckets /auth/* (startsWith("/auth/")) but never /admin/auth/login or /admin/auth/refresh, so it returns null and the request is unthrottled. Only the per-account lockout in AdminAuthService.login (5 per 15 min, and 3 per hour for MFA) applies. That permits unlimited password spraying across admin emails, and lets anyone lock known admins out on demand.
questions.evidence: Code read of every bucketFor branch; no admin/auth string in AuthRateLimitFilter.java.
questions.remaining_uncertainty: An edge WAF/Cloudflare rule might throttle this path; none is in the repo.

questions.question: Is the rate limiter's client IP the real client behind the proxy chain in deploy/**?
questions.why_it_matters: Every IP-keyed bucket (login 10/min, OTP, refresh, portfolio contact, festival enquiries) and the admin audit-log IP depend on it.
questions.answer: Hostinger (Caddy is the public edge): yes. deploy/utho: probably not. The chain is nginx (host, appends $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for, nginx-influora.conf:69) -> 127.0.0.1:8080 -> Caddy in Docker (caddy:2-alpine, no trusted_proxies in deploy/utho/Caddyfile, so Caddy discards the incoming XFF and sets it to its immediate peer, the Docker gateway) -> Tomcat RemoteIpValve with internal-proxies = RFC1918 (application.yml:90,116). Every hop is 'internal', so getRemoteAddr() (AuthRateLimitFilter.java:703-704) resolves to the Docker gateway for all users. The 10/min login bucket becomes platform-wide: an easy DoS, and it misattributes IPs in audit records.
questions.evidence: Config read of Caddyfile, nginx confs, compose and application.yml, reasoned against documented Caddy >=2.5 and RemoteIpValve behaviour.
questions.remaining_uncertainty: The live Utho stack is /usr/local/App/docker-compose.prod.yml, which is not in the repo. The Caddy version and Docker userland-proxy setting on the host are unverified.

questions.question: Can an unauthenticated caller enumerate accounts?
questions.why_it_matters: Targeted phishing and credential stuffing on a two-sided marketplace.
questions.answer: Yes. AuthService.brandLogin (AuthService.java:262-264) and creatorLogin (~:477) throw WRONG_USER_TYPE (403) BEFORE the password check, so any email reveals whether it exists and whether it is a brand or a creator. Register also returns EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS (AuthService.java:128, 365). An unknown email skips bcrypt, which leaves a timing oracle. forgot-password is correctly generic.
questions.remaining_uncertainty: The 'sensitive' bucket bounds the rate (10/min/IP) but does not remove the oracle.

questions.question: Are JWT signing, algorithm handling, expiry and refresh rotation sound?
questions.why_it_matters: This is the core authentication boundary.
questions.answer: Mostly yes. HMAC key from influora.jwt.access-secret (application.yml:203), which fails closed outside dev on known defaults (SecretsStartupValidator.java:132-135, 283-353). jjwt verifyWith(SecretKey) rejects alg=none and mismatched algorithms. Access TTL 900s; refresh is an opaque random value, stored hashed, rotated on use (AuthService.java:535-642) with suspension, workspace and verification checks. Gaps: no refresh-reuse detection (a presented revoked token does not revoke the family); JwtAuthenticationFilter never touches the DB, so deleted, suspended or removed users keep up to 15 minutes of access, and requireBrandWorkspace trusts the JWT workspaceId claim without an active-membership check (BrandContextService.java:72-110; 70 methods use it without requireMember).
questions.evidence: Code read of JwtService, JwtAuthenticationFilter, AuthService.refresh and BrandContextService; AuthServiceTest 64/64 and SpringJwksKeyServiceTest 11/11 green in target/surefire-reports.
questions.remaining_uncertainty: Surefire reports were produced by another agent's run in the RC dir; I did not re-run them.

questions.question: Do webhooks verify authenticity and resist amount manipulation?
questions.why_it_matters: Forged payment webhooks would mint wallet balance.
questions.answer: Yes. Razorpay: HMAC-SHA256, constant-time compare, fail-closed on a blank secret (WebhookSignatureVerifier.java:26-36); the placeholder secret is refused outside dev. confirmCredited locks the row, is idempotent and validates the webhook amount against the stored order (WalletTopUpService.java:182-227). The escrow fund amount is derived server-side (EscrowController.java:81-83). Shopify, WooCommerce, conversion and Meta callbacks all use constant-time verification.
questions.evidence: Code read; RazorpayWebhookControllerTest 13/13, Shopify/Woo/Conversion verifier tests 10/10 each, green in surefire reports.
questions.remaining_uncertainty: There is no timestamp/replay window; idempotency covers top-up and escrow, but replay of old payout.* events was not traced.

questions.question: Is there SQL/JPQL injection, XSS, or unsafe file upload?
questions.why_it_matters: These are classic OWASP A03 and A04 risks.
questions.answer: None found. Native queries (CampaignServiceInvoiceService.java:306-502, ProvisionSuperAdminRunner.java:316) use bound parameters, and sort fields are whitelisted (CampaignService.java:630-639). On the frontend, dangerouslySetInnerHTML appears only in chart.tsx (static CSS) and JsonLd (escapes '<', schema.ts:266); the admin email preview is a sandbox="" iframe. Uploads use magic-byte sniffing (images, video, PDF only; no SVG/HTML), a declared-vs-sniffed type match, a server-generated key (uploads/<type>/<userId>/<ULID>.<ext>), ClamAV under @Profile(prod), and KYC purposes stored privately.
questions.evidence: Grep plus code read; UploadServiceTest 13/13 and ClamAvMalwareScanServiceTest 5/5 green.
questions.remaining_uncertainty: Not every frontend markdown/Meera rendering path was traced.

questions.question: Can a server-side fetch be steered to internal addresses (SSRF)?
questions.why_it_matters: Cloud metadata endpoints and internal services (Spring /internal, MySQL) sit on the same network.
questions.answer: Protected. Brand URLs are fetched only in influora-ai via guarded_fetch: https only, DNS resolved then pinned, every resolved IP checked against private, loopback, link-local, CGNAT and metadata ranges, at most 2 redirects each re-validated, plus size and time caps (influora-ai/app/security/ssrf_guard.py:36-128). Shopify shop domains are regex-locked to *.myshopify.com (ShopifyOAuthService.java:54-81). Tracking-link baseUrl is validated (CampaignLinkService.java:174, 273).
questions.remaining_uncertainty: Python SSRF tests were not executed in this pass.

questions.question: Do secrets or sensitive tokens leak through logs or third parties?
questions.why_it_matters: It sets the blast radius of any analytics or log exposure.
questions.answer: No secret values appear in Spring or Python logs outside dev-gated lines (AuthService.java:869-874, BrandEmailOtpService.java:313). But password-reset links (AuthService.java:881, 1h TTL, 7 days for sponsor provisioning) and workspace invite links carry the raw token in the query string. The SPA reads it without stripping it (brand-reset-password.tsx:22, brand-accept-invite.tsx:29), and public/site-tags.js loads GTM unconditionally on every route. GA4 page_location, the Clarity session URL and the Meta Pixel 'dl' parameter would carry the token to Google, Microsoft and Meta.
questions.evidence: Code read of the site-tags.js loader, the reset/invite pages and the link builder.
questions.remaining_uncertainty: The GTM container configuration is not in the repo; a URL-redaction variable in GTM would mitigate this.

questions.question: Are CORS and CSRF correctly configured for a bearer-plus-refresh-cookie design?
questions.why_it_matters: It determines whether any cross-site request can act as the user.
questions.answer: Yes. CorsConfig uses an explicit origin list from CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS (compose sets the https app/root domains) with credentials; there is no wildcard. CSRF is disabled, which is justified because authorization is the Bearer header and the only cookie is the HttpOnly refresh cookie scoped to /auth. A cross-site POST /auth/refresh cannot read the returned token.
questions.remaining_uncertainty: The SameSite value is env-driven; SecretsStartupValidator.validateRefreshCookieSecureFlags checks it.

findings.title: Live-format third-party credentials committed in tracked env.example files (Anthropic, Sarvam, Cloudflare R2, MSG91)
findings.evidence: influora-ai/env.example:12 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=[REDACTED] (108 chars, sk-ant- prefix, ends AA, entropy 5.49, no placeholder markers). influora-ai/env.example:19 SARVAM_API_KEY=[REDACTED] (36 chars, high entropy). influora-api/env.example:50 R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID=[REDACTED] (32 hex) and :51 R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=[REDACTED] (64 hex), exactly the Cloudflare R2 format. influora-api/env.example:67 MSG91_AUTH_KEY=[REDACTED] and :71 MSG91_TOKEN_AUTH=[REDACTED] (27 alnum). The same values appear in git history of influora-ai/env.example at b63ccf3, 2d0e1bd, e3e59d0, 1792c37, 8c7b18b; influora-api/env.example history is b63ccf3, 8c7b18b, 864971a.
findings.impact: Anyone with read access to the repo, or to any fork, clone or CI log, can spend on the Anthropic and Sarvam accounts, read and write the R2 bucket (brand logos, deliverables and, via the private path, KYC documents), and send email/SMS as Influora through MSG91 (phishing from a trusted sender, and OTP abuse).
findings.recommended_fix: Rotate all four providers' keys now: revoke at Anthropic, Sarvam, Cloudflare R2 and MSG91, and treat the old values as compromised. Replace the file values with obvious placeholders (e.g. REPLACE_ME). Purge them from history (git filter-repo) or accept that the history stays compromised. Add a secret-scanning pre-commit/CI gate (gitleaks) covering *.example files.
findings.verification_required: The owner confirms in each provider console whether the committed keys are or were active and checks their usage logs. After rotation, rerun git grep and gitleaks on HEAD and history.
findings.reproduction: From the RC dir: python shape/entropy check on the listed lines (values never printed).

findings.title: /internal/** service-mesh gate bypassed by percent-encoded path; any logged-in user can refund Meera turn credits and forge assistant messages
findings.evidence: InternalServiceTokenFilter.java:82-83: `String path = stripContext(request.getRequestURI()); if (!path.startsWith(INTERNAL_PREFIX)) { chain.doFilter(...); return; }`. The URI is raw and never decoded. AuthRateLimitFilter already decodes for this exact bypass class (its javadoc cites Kabir NEW-1), but this filter was never given the same fix. MeeraInternalController (e.g. :319 persistTurnWriteback, :354 releaseTurnCredit) never checks that the principal is InternalPrincipal/ROLE_INTERNAL_SERVICE. SecurityConfig.java:298-299 requires only authenticated() for /internal/**, which a normal user JWT satisfies. The on-behalf token is handed to the browser (MeeraSessionService.java:441-448, TurnResult.onBehalfToken). AICreditService.release (AICreditService.java:263-293) refunds any charged turnId in the workspace, once, with no check that the turn failed. Runtime probe against the real spring-web 6.1.14 and spring-security-web 6.3.4 jars: `/api/v1/%69nternal/meera/turns/release firewall=ALLOWED internalFilterRuns=false mvcRoutesToController=true`.
findings.impact: Any brand or creator can call internal Meera routes for their own workspace without the service token and HMAC. Consequences: (a) POST %69nternal/meera/turns/release after each turn refunds every AI credit, giving unlimited Meera usage on the platform's Anthropic bill; (b) POST .../messages persists attacker-authored 'assistant' turns; (c) tool routes run outside the Python tool loop's validation. Cross-tenant access is still blocked by OnBehalfAuthResolver's workspace binding.
findings.recommended_fix: In InternalServiceTokenFilter, match on the decoded, normalised path, as AuthRateLimitFilter does with decode() and stripMatrixParams(); or better, register it with a Spring RequestMatcher/securityMatcher for /internal/** so it shares MVC's decoding. As defence in depth, add .requestMatchers("/internal/**").hasRole("INTERNAL_SERVICE") in SecurityConfig so a user JWT can never authorise an internal route. Add a MockMvc test that sends /api/v1/%69nternal/meera/turns/release with a user JWT and asserts 401/403.
findings.verification_required: Kavya/Meera run a MockMvc or booted-app test sending %69nternal with a brand JWT and a valid on-behalf token and observe a 200 today. Also confirm whether Caddy/nginx forward the escaped path unchanged in the live topology.
findings.reproduction: Scratchpad probe Probe.java (StrictHttpFirewall + ServletRequestPathUtils + PathPatternParser 'matches' against '/internal/meera/turns/release'), compiled against ~/.m2 spring-web 6.1.14, spring-security-web 6.3.4 and tomcat-embed-core 10.1.31.
affected_features: Meera internal tools (create_campaign, request_payment, confirm_launch, show_creators, calculate_budget, get_campaign_performance, context)

findings.title: Any workspace member (including VIEWER) can approve a deliverable, and approval releases escrow funds, bypassing the OWNER/ADMIN release gate
findings.evidence: BrandDeliverableService.approve (BrandDeliverableService.java:128-187) calls only brandContext.requireBrandWorkspace(principal) (JWT workspace claim, no membership or role) and then escrowService.tryReleaseOnApproval(workspace.getId(), deliverable.getMilestoneId()) at ~:187. The explicit EscrowService.release requires requireMember plus requireRole(OWNER, ADMIN) (EscrowService.java:593-595). MemberRole = OWNER/ADMIN/MANAGER/MEMBER/VIEWER. No test asserts a role on approve.
findings.impact: A VIEWER or MEMBER seat, or a removed member within the 15-minute access-token window, can move brand escrow to a creator. That defeats the brand's own separation of duties and enables collusion between a low-privilege seat and a creator.
findings.recommended_fix: In approve (and reject/requestRevision), call brandContext.requireMember(principal, workspace.getId()) and requireRole(member, OWNER, ADMIN[, MANAGER if product agrees]), matching the release gate. Add a test asserting VIEWER/MEMBER get 403 and that no ledger movement occurs.
findings.verification_required: Unit test with a VIEWER member mocked on BrandContextService showing approve currently succeeds and tryReleaseOnApproval is invoked.
findings.reproduction: POST /api/v1/brand/deliverables/{id}/approve with a VIEWER member's JWT on a SUBMITTED deliverable whose milestone is funded.

findings.title: Admin MFA secret can be overwritten while MFA is enabled (no current-code or password re-verification)
findings.evidence: AdminAuthService.setupMfa (AdminAuthService.java:278-291) always runs admin.stageMfaSecret(mfaSecretCipher.encrypt(secret)), which sets encryptedMfaSecret unconditionally (AdminUser.java:242-245), and returns the plaintext secret. There is no isMfaEnabled() guard and no current TOTP or password check. login() verifies TOTP against getEncryptedMfaSecret() (AdminAuthService.java:152), so the new secret takes effect immediately. The route is POST /admin/auth/mfa/setup (AdminAuthController.java:114-118), reachable with any admin access token. Admin tokens are stored in localStorage (src/admin/services/admin-session.ts:107). No test covers setupMfa.
findings.impact: A stolen or XSS'd 15-minute admin access token becomes a durable second factor bound to the attacker's authenticator. Even the setup call alone invalidates the real admin's authenticator, so they cannot log in until a SUPER_ADMIN resets them.
findings.recommended_fix: Reject setupMfa when mfaEnabled is true (require the SUPER_ADMIN reset path), or require a valid code from the CURRENT secret plus the password. Stage the new secret in a separate pending column and promote it only in verifyMfa. Audit-log MFA changes and notify the admin by email.
findings.verification_required: Unit test: an enrolled admin calls setupMfa and login with the old TOTP now fails (demonstrates the defect); after the fix, setupMfa returns 409.
findings.reproduction: With an enrolled admin's access token: POST /api/v1/admin/auth/mfa/setup; enrol the returned secret; POST /mfa/verify; the original authenticator no longer works.

findings.title: Admin login and refresh have no IP rate-limit bucket
findings.evidence: AuthRateLimitFilter.bucketFor (AuthRateLimitFilter.java:342-512) throttles path.startsWith("/auth/") as 'sensitive' but has no branch for /admin/auth/login or /admin/auth/refresh, so it returns null and the request passes unthrottled (lines 295-298). Only the per-account lockout in AdminAuthService.login applies.
findings.impact: Unlimited password spraying across admin emails from one IP, and deliberate lockout of every known admin (5 wrong passwords per 15 minutes per account) with no per-source cost.
findings.recommended_fix: Add `if (path.equals("/admin/auth/login") || path.equals("/admin/auth/refresh")) return "sensitive";` (or a tighter dedicated bucket) plus a test, and consider an IP allow-list or VPN for the admin host.
findings.verification_required: Add an AuthRateLimitFilter test that sends 11 POSTs to /api/v1/admin/auth/login and expects a 429; it passes 200s today.
findings.reproduction: Loop POST /api/v1/admin/auth/login with a wrong password; no X-RateLimit headers or 429 are ever returned.

findings.title: deploy/utho proxy chain likely collapses every client IP to the Docker gateway, making per-IP limits global
findings.evidence: deploy/utho/nginx-influora.conf:69 appends XFF and proxies to 127.0.0.1:8080. docker-compose.utho.yml:62-63 publishes Caddy on 127.0.0.1:8080 (caddy:2-alpine). deploy/utho/Caddyfile:39 uses reverse_proxy influora-api:8080 with no trusted_proxies, so Caddy >=2.5 ignores the incoming XFF from its untrusted peer and sets it to the peer IP (the Docker bridge gateway). application.yml:90 forward-headers-strategy native and :116 RemoteIpValve internal-proxies = RFC1918 + loopback, so every hop is internal. AuthRateLimitFilter.clientIp returns request.getRemoteAddr() (AuthRateLimitFilter.java:703-704), and AdminAuditLogService uses the same value.
findings.impact: The login 'sensitive' bucket (10/min), OTP (5/min), refresh (30/min), portfolio-contact, festival and client-errors buckets become platform-wide. One attacker, or a traffic spike, returns 429 to every user's login and OTP. Admin audit IPs all show the gateway.
findings.recommended_fix: In the Utho Caddyfile global options add `servers { trusted_proxies static 127.0.0.1/32 172.16.0.0/12 }` (the nginx hop) so Caddy keeps nginx's XFF; make nginx overwrite rather than append (`proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr;`, or real_ip from Cloudflare if the host is proxied); verify with a debug endpoint or a log of getRemoteAddr().
findings.verification_required: On the live host, log request.getRemoteAddr() for two requests from different IPs, or read the X-RateLimit-Remaining header from two different networks, and confirm whether they share one bucket.
findings.reproduction: Two clients on different networks each POST /auth/brand/login once, and the second sees X-RateLimit-Remaining decremented by the first.

findings.title: Login endpoints disclose account existence and account type before password verification
findings.evidence: AuthService.brandLogin (AuthService.java:262-264) throws WRONG_USER_TYPE 403 'This endpoint is for brand accounts only' before passwordEncoder.matches. creatorLogin does the mirror (~:477). An unknown email returns INVALID_CREDENTIALS without running bcrypt (timing difference). Register returns EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS (AuthService.java:128, 365).
findings.impact: An anonymous caller can confirm, with any password, that an email is a registered brand or creator. That enables targeted phishing and credential stuffing, and it leaks who uses the marketplace.
findings.recommended_fix: Move the user-type check after a successful password match and return the same INVALID_CREDENTIALS for both cases; run a dummy bcrypt on an unknown email. Accept or mitigate the register enumeration with a verify-email-first flow.
findings.verification_required: Unit test: brandLogin with a creator's email and a wrong password should return INVALID_CREDENTIALS 401; today it returns WRONG_USER_TYPE 403.
findings.reproduction: POST /api/v1/auth/brand/login {email: <known creator email>, password: 'x'} returns 403 WRONG_USER_TYPE.

findings.title: Password-reset and workspace-invite tokens are sent in URL query strings on pages that load GTM (GA4, Clarity, Meta Pixel)
findings.evidence: AuthService.createPasswordResetToken builds webBaseUrl + "/reset-password?token=" + raw (AuthService.java:881; 1h TTL, and 7 days via FestivalSponsorProvisioningService#issuePasswordSetLink). src/pages/brand-reset-password.tsx:22 and src/pages/brand-accept-invite.tsx:29 read the token from the query string and never history.replaceState it away (the only replaceState is in creator-meta-callback.tsx:126). public/site-tags.js injects GTM-K7LNG26G unconditionally on every route (index.html:66-80).
findings.impact: Live, single-use account-takeover tokens reach third-party analytics (GA4 page_location, the Clarity recording URL, Meta Pixel dl) and are visible to anyone with access to those consoles for the token's lifetime.
findings.recommended_fix: Use a URL fragment (#token=), which is not sent to servers or in page_location by default, or strip the token with history.replaceState before site-tags.js loads; skip GTM on /reset-password and /accept-invite routes; add a GTM URL-redaction variable for token/code/state params.
findings.verification_required: Open a reset link in a browser with devtools and confirm whether a request to google-analytics.com/clarity.ms/facebook.com carries the token (safe: use a dev/staging token).
findings.reproduction: Visit /reset-password?token=TEST on a build with GTM enabled and inspect the network requests for 'TEST'.

findings.title: Missing workspace role checks: any member can sign contracts as the brand and rotate or read the conversion-webhook HMAC secret
findings.evidence: ContractService.recordSignature (ContractService.java:897-904) calls requireMember only, while generate (:146-148), amend (:441-444) and cancel (:1030-1033) require OWNER/ADMIN/MANAGER. ConversionWebhookSecretController.generate (:50-53) and revoke (:63-66) call only requireBrandWorkspace (JWT claim; no membership or role) and generate returns the plaintext secret (ConversionWebhookSecretDtos.java:21).
findings.impact: A VIEWER can legally bind the brand to a contract. A VIEWER, or a removed member within 15 minutes, can rotate the secret, silently breaking the brand's conversion integration, or learn it and forge signed /webhooks/conversion and /webhooks/redemption events for that workspace, poisoning attribution/ROI data and any commission derived from it.
findings.recommended_fix: Add requireMember + requireRole(OWNER, ADMIN[, MANAGER]) to recordSignature (BRAND side) and to both webhook-secret routes. More generally, make requireBrandWorkspace also assert active membership (70 methods rely on it alone).
findings.verification_required: Unit tests with a VIEWER member on each route expecting 403.
findings.reproduction: POST /api/v1/webhook-secret/generate with a VIEWER's JWT returns 200 with the plaintext secret.

findings.title: Account deletion requires no re-authentication, and access tokens survive deletion, suspension and member removal for up to 15 minutes
findings.evidence: AccountController.deleteAccount (AccountController.java:79-106) soft-deletes on the bearer token alone, with no password or OTP. JwtAuthenticationFilter.doFilterInternal (JwtAuthenticationFilter.java:17-47 of that file) is a pure signature parse with no DB check. BrandContextService.requireBrandWorkspace (BrandContextService.java:72-110) trusts principal.getWorkspaceId() without checking active membership.
findings.impact: A stolen access token (tokens live in localStorage) can irreversibly delete the victim's account. Removed members and deleted users keep API access to requireBrandWorkspace-only endpoints for up to 900s.
findings.recommended_fix: Require currentPassword (or an email OTP) on DELETE /me/account. In requireBrandWorkspace, verify findByWorkspaceIdAndUserIdAndActiveTrue. Optionally keep a small deny-list keyed by jti/userId on deletion or removal.
findings.verification_required: Test: a DELETE /me/account without a password currently succeeds.
findings.reproduction: DELETE /api/v1/me/account with only a Bearer token returns 200.

findings.title: Refresh-token rotation has no reuse detection
findings.evidence: AuthService.refresh (AuthService.java:535-642) and AdminAuthService.refresh (AdminAuthService.java:225-262) look up findByTokenHashAndRevokedFalse. A replayed, already-rotated token simply returns 401 and the rest of the token family is not revoked.
findings.impact: If a refresh token is stolen and the thief refreshes first, the legitimate user's next refresh fails, but the thief's chain stays valid for up to 30 days (users) with no alert.
findings.recommended_fix: When a revoked-but-known token hash is presented, revoke all of that user's refresh tokens (family revocation) and audit-log the event.
findings.verification_required: Unit test that replays a rotated token and asserts every token for the user is revoked.
findings.reproduction: Refresh with token A, which yields B; replay A (401); B is still valid.

findings.title: Rate-limit window map is never evicted (unbounded memory growth keyed by client IP)
findings.evidence: AuthRateLimitFilter.java:283 `private final Map<String, Window> windows = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();`. The only access is windows.compute at :306; there is no remove, no scheduled cleanup and no size bound.
findings.impact: Every distinct IP|bucket or user|bucket key lives forever. An IPv6 attacker rotating source addresses grows the heap without bound until the JVM runs out of memory.
findings.recommended_fix: Use a Caffeine cache with expireAfterWrite(window) and maximumSize, or a periodic sweep of windows older than their bucket window.
findings.verification_required: A unit test hitting 100k distinct remoteAddr values and checking the map size.

findings.title: One-click unsubscribe mutates state on GET
findings.evidence: NotificationController.unsubscribeViaLink (NotificationController.java:192-219) is GET /notifications/unsubscribe-link and calls preference.setUnsubscribed(true) and emailPreferenceRepository.save. The HTML response itself is static (no reflection).
findings.impact: Corporate mail scanners and link-prefetchers that GET every link will silently unsubscribe users from transactional categories.
findings.recommended_fix: GET should render a confirm page and a POST should perform the change; support RFC 8058 List-Unsubscribe-Post.
findings.verification_required: Manual check against a link-scanning mail provider.
findings.reproduction: curl -I the unsubscribe link and observe the preference flipped.
